name: Calibration curve
seoDesc: Calibration curve: work out sensitivity (a) from the background and the signal. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: sensitivity (a) is what the Calibration curve calculator works out, and it gets there from the background, the signal and the concentration. That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Calibration curve calculator work?
sections.html:
The Calibration curve calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports sensitivity (a) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the background (b), the signal (y) and the concentration (x).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Calibration curve calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Sensitivity (a)=(-background (b) + signal (y)) ÷ concentration (x)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Calibration curve calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the background, the signal and the concentration — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Calibration curve calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — background for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Calibration curve calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns sensitivity (a), derived from the background, the signal and the concentration. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Calibration curve calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the background, the signal and the concentration, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Calibration curve calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
